sourceApproval: Founder-approved under DEC-040 (adapted to Physics Academy rigor)
prerequisites: Lesson 2 — the slope of a graph is rise over run; the slope of a position-time graph is velocity.
Lesson 3 — velocity is signed; on a velocity-time graph a horizontal segment is constant velocity; $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$ is the area of that segment.
majorObjective: Read a velocity-time graph quantitatively: the slope of a segment is the acceleration, the signed area between the graph and the time axis is the displacement, and a described motion can be matched to the correctly shaped velocity-time graph.
subObjectives: Calculate the slope $\Delta v / \Delta t$ of a velocity-time segment and interpret it as an acceleration, including for a segment that crosses zero velocity.
Calculate displacement as the area under a velocity-time segment — a rectangle for constant velocity, a triangle for constant acceleration.
Combine areas above and below the time axis as a signed sum to get a net displacement.
Match a verbal description of a motion to a velocity-time graph by checking sign, constancy, and pattern of change one element at a time.

hook.prompt: A velocity-time graph is a straight line from $+6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ down to $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ over $4\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the slope, and does the calculation change at the moment the line crosses zero?
choices: Slope $= -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$; the calculation is the same right through the zero crossing.
Slope $= -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ before the crossing and $+2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ after it.
Slope $= -8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$; the crossing has no effect.
The slope is undefined at the instant the line crosses zero.

priorKnowledge: On a velocity-time graph the height is the signed velocity. This lesson adds the two quantitative readings: the slope (a rate of change of velocity, i.e. acceleration) and the signed area (a displacement).

chunks.title: The slope of a velocity-time segment is the acceleration
chunks.concept:
The **slope** of a straight velocity-time segment is the rate at which the velocity is changing: $$\text{slope} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1}$$ Its unit is $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ — metres per second, per second. This rate is the **acceleration** (the next lesson defines acceleration formally; here it is just this slope).

A segment that **crosses zero velocity** — an object slowing to a stop and then moving off the other way — is a good stress test. Nothing special happens to the slope calculation at the crossing point: you still take one point before and one point after and divide. The line stays straight right through $v = 0$.
chunks.representation:
To get the slope of a velocity-time segment:

1. Pick two points on the same straight segment.
2. Rise: $\Delta v = v_2 - v_1$, keeping the sign.
3. Run: $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$, always positive.
4. Divide, and attach $\mathrm{m/s^2}$. A downward-sloping segment gives a negative rate whether or not it crosses zero.

conceptFigures.caption: The segment runs from $+6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ over $4\ \mathrm{s}$: slope $= -8/4 = -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. It crosses $v = 0$ at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$, and the slope is the same on both sides.

workedExample.problem: From the graph above, find the acceleration on the segment, and state what the object is doing just before and just after $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$.

phases.label: Read two points and take rise over run
Divide
steps: $\text{slope} = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{-8\ \mathrm{m/s}}{4\ \mathrm{s}} = -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ — a constant acceleration in the negative direction.

phases.label: Describe the motion around the crossing
steps: Before $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$: velocity is positive and shrinking — moving in the positive direction, slowing down.
After $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$: velocity is negative and growing in size — now moving in the negative direction, speeding up. The acceleration was $-2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ the whole time.

workedExample.keyMove: The zero crossing changes what the object is doing, but not the slope — read the slope from any two points on the segment.

formativeCheck.question: A velocity-time segment goes from $(1\ \mathrm{s},\ -4\ \mathrm{m/s})$ to $(5\ \mathrm{s},\ +8\ \mathrm{m/s})$. What is the acceleration?

incorrect.1: The velocity rises as time goes on, so the slope is positive. Check the order: later value minus earlier value.
incorrect.2: $+12\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is the rise $\Delta v$ alone. Divide by the run $\Delta t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$.
incorrect.3: The run is $5 - 1 = 4\ \mathrm{s}$, but the rise is $(+8) - (-4) = +12$, not $+16$. Subtracting a negative adds.

hint: $\Delta v = v_2 - v_1$ with the later point second. Subtracting $-4$ adds $4$.

chunks.title: The signed area is the displacement
chunks.concept:
The **area between a velocity-time segment and the time axis** is the displacement over that interval.

- A **constant-velocity** segment gives a **rectangle**: $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t = \text{height} \times \text{base}$.
- A **constant-acceleration** segment gives a **triangle** (or a rectangle plus a triangle): area $= \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{base} \times \text{height}$ for the triangular part.

Area **below** the time axis is **negative** displacement. When a graph has regions both above and below the axis, do not make the lower area positive and add it — combine the regions as a **signed sum**. The result is the net change in position, which can be smaller than either piece or even zero.
chunks.representation:
For a multi-region velocity-time graph:

1. Split it into rectangles and triangles.
2. Find each area, and attach a $+$ sign if the region is above the axis, a $-$ sign if below.
3. Add the signed areas.
4. The total is the net displacement; its sign is the overall direction.

conceptFigures.caption: Above the axis: $(+5\ \mathrm{m/s})(2\ \mathrm{s}) = +10\ \mathrm{m}$. Below the axis: $(-3\ \mathrm{m/s})(4\ \mathrm{s}) = -12\ \mathrm{m}$. Net displacement $= (+10) + (-12) = -2\ \mathrm{m}$.

workedExample.problem: An object's velocity-time graph has two segments: $+8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (constant) from $0$ to $3\ \mathrm{s}$, then a straight fall from $+8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $0$ over the next $2\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the total displacement from $0$ to $5\ \mathrm{s}$.

phases.label: Second segment — a triangle
steps: The velocity drops from $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $0$ over $2\ \mathrm{s}$ — a triangle with base $2\ \mathrm{s}$ and height $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
Area $= \tfrac{1}{2}(2)(8) = +8\ \mathrm{m}$ (still above the axis, so positive).

phases.label: Add the signed areas
steps: $\Delta x = (+24\ \mathrm{m}) + (+8\ \mathrm{m}) = +32\ \mathrm{m}$ — the object finishes $32\ \mathrm{m}$ in the positive direction.

workedExample.keyMove: Rectangle for the constant part, triangle for the sloped part; sign each by which side of the axis it is on, then add.

formativeCheck.question: A velocity-time graph is $+4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (constant) from $0$ to $3\ \mathrm{s}$, then $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (constant) from $3\ \mathrm{s}$ to $9\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the net displacement over the whole $9\ \mathrm{s}$?

incorrect.1: This adds the magnitudes ($12 + 24$) as if both regions were positive. The region below the axis is negative displacement.
incorrect.2: The two regions do not cancel: the negative segment lasts $6\ \mathrm{s}$, twice as long as the positive one, so its area is larger.
incorrect.3: $+12\ \mathrm{m}$ is just the first region. The second region ($-24\ \mathrm{m}$) more than cancels it.

hint: Area above the axis is positive, area below is negative. The below region is $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $6\ \mathrm{s}$.
formativeCheck.solution: Above the axis: $(+4\ \mathrm{m/s})(3\ \mathrm{s}) = +12\ \mathrm{m}$. Below the axis: $(-4\ \mathrm{m/s})(6\ \mathrm{s}) = -24\ \mathrm{m}$. Net displacement $= (+12) + (-24) = -12\ \mathrm{m}$.

chunks.title: Matching a description to a velocity-time graph
chunks.concept:
To choose the right velocity-time graph for a described motion, break the description into **three separate checks** and test a candidate graph against each:

- **Sign** — is the velocity positive, negative, or does it change sign?
- **Constancy** — is the velocity holding steady (horizontal) or changing (sloped)?
- **Pattern of change** — if it is changing, how? Uniform slowing, a brief rest, uniform speeding up the other way, and so on.

A candidate graph has to pass **all three**. Checking them one at a time is faster and more reliable than trying to picture the whole graph at once.
chunks.representation:
Turn the words into graph features:

- “moving forward / backward” → segment above / below the axis.
- “steady speed” → horizontal segment.
- “slowing to a stop” → sloped segment heading toward the axis.
- “stopped for a moment” → the graph touches the axis (it need not flatten).
- “speeding up the other way” → the segment continues past the axis with the same slope.

workedExample.problem: A cart moves in the positive direction, slows uniformly to a stop, and then speeds up uniformly in the negative direction — all at the same rate. Describe the velocity-time graph, element by element.

phases.label: Sign
steps: It starts moving positive, ends moving negative, so the graph starts above the axis and finishes below it — it must cross the axis once.

phases.label: Constancy
steps: The velocity is changing the whole time (slowing, then speeding up), so the graph is sloped, not horizontal, throughout.

phases.label: Pattern of change
steps: “Uniformly … at the same rate” means one constant slope. So the graph is a single straight line running from a positive value, down through zero, to a negative value — it does not bend or flatten at the crossing.

workedExample.keyMove: One straight sloped line through the axis — the description of “slow down, stop, reverse at the same rate” is exactly a constant slope.

formativeCheck.question: An object travels in the positive direction at a steady speed, then abruptly stops and stays at rest. Which velocity-time graph matches?
choices: A horizontal segment above the axis, then a horizontal segment on the axis.
A horizontal segment above the axis, then a horizontal segment below the axis.
A single sloped line from a positive value down to zero.
A horizontal segment on the axis, then a horizontal segment above it.

feedback.correct: Correct — steady positive speed is a horizontal segment above the axis; at rest is a horizontal segment sitting on the axis ($v = 0$).

incorrect.1: A segment below the axis means moving in the negative direction. The object stops, it does not reverse.
incorrect.2: A sloped line means the velocity changes gradually. This object stops abruptly, and “steady speed” before that is horizontal, not sloped.
incorrect.3: This has the object at rest first and then moving — the reverse of the description.

hint: Steady speed → horizontal. Moving forward → above the axis. At rest → on the axis.
formativeCheck.solution: Steady speed in the positive direction is a horizontal segment above the time axis. Coming to rest and staying there is a horizontal segment exactly on the time axis ($v = 0$). No part of the motion is in the negative direction, so nothing goes below the axis.

misconceptions.question: A velocity-time graph is $+6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $2\ \mathrm{s}$, then $-6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $2\ \mathrm{s}$. A student says the total displacement is $24\ \mathrm{m}$ “because the two areas are each $12\ \mathrm{m}$ and $12 + 12 = 24$.” What is the correct total displacement?
choices: $0\ \mathrm{m}$ — the area below the axis is $-12\ \mathrm{m}$, and $(+12) + (-12) = 0$.

feedback.correct: Correct — the first region is $+12\ \mathrm{m}$ (above the axis) and the second is $-12\ \mathrm{m}$ (below). The signed sum is $0$: the object returns to its starting position.

incorrect.0: The student added the magnitudes. Area below the time axis represents negative displacement and must be subtracted, not added as a positive.
incorrect.2: The second region is real displacement too — it just happens to be negative. Both regions count.
incorrect.3: Only the second region is below the axis. The first is above it and positive.

hint: The two regions are on opposite sides of the time axis. What sign does each displacement have?
misconceptions.solution: Displacement is the signed area. Region 1: $(+6\ \mathrm{m/s})(2\ \mathrm{s}) = +12\ \mathrm{m}$. Region 2: $(-6\ \mathrm{m/s})(2\ \mathrm{s}) = -12\ \mathrm{m}$. Net $= (+12) + (-12) = 0\ \mathrm{m}$ — the object ends where it began. The total distance travelled is $24\ \mathrm{m}$, but that is not the displacement.

errorAnalysis.studentWork:
Problem: A velocity-time graph is $+10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (constant) from $0$ to $2\ \mathrm{s}$, then $-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (constant) from $2\ \mathrm{s}$ to $8\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the net displacement.

Student's response: “First area: $10 \times 2 = 20\ \mathrm{m}$. Second area: $5 \times 6 = 30\ \mathrm{m}$. Total displacement $= 20 + 30 = 50\ \mathrm{m}$.”
prompts: State the rule for the sign of an area that lies below the time axis.
Identify the first step that is not supported by that rule.
Repair the response: give the correct net displacement with its sign, and check it against the two regions.
errorAnalysis.modelResponse: The rule: an area below the time axis is a negative displacement — it is subtracted, not added as a positive. The first unsupported step is “Second area $= 5 \times 6 = 30\ \mathrm{m}$” written as a positive: the segment is at $-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$, below the axis, so that area is $-30\ \mathrm{m}$. Correct: net displacement $= (+20\ \mathrm{m}) + (-30\ \mathrm{m}) = -10\ \mathrm{m}$. Check: the object went $+20\ \mathrm{m}$ forward, then $30\ \mathrm{m}$ back, finishing $10\ \mathrm{m}$ behind the start — a negative net displacement, which matches.

representationConnections: A verbal motion becomes a velocity-time graph; the graph's slope is the acceleration (a rate, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$); the graph's signed area is the displacement (an accumulation, in $\mathrm{m}$); and the three verbal checks — sign, constancy, pattern of change — are exactly the three features that fix the graph's shape. Slope and area are the same two operations you met for position-time graphs, one level up.

lessonAssessment.question: On a velocity-time graph, a segment is horizontal at $-3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $5\ \mathrm{s}$. Which pair of statements is correct?

feedback.correct: Correct — a horizontal segment has zero slope, so acceleration $= 0$. The area is $(-3\ \mathrm{m/s})(5\ \mathrm{s}) = -15\ \mathrm{m}$, below the axis.

incorrect.1: $-3$ is the velocity, not the acceleration. A horizontal segment has zero slope, so the acceleration is $0$.
incorrect.2: The segment is below the time axis, so the displacement is negative: $-15\ \mathrm{m}$, not $+15\ \mathrm{m}$.
incorrect.3: Dividing $-3$ by $5$ is not how you get either quantity here. Slope is zero (horizontal); area is height times base.

hint: Horizontal segment → slope (acceleration) is zero. Area → height $\times$ base, signed by which side of the axis.
lessonAssessment.solution: A horizontal segment has zero slope, so the acceleration is $0$. The displacement is the area: $(-3\ \mathrm{m/s}) \times (5\ \mathrm{s}) = -15\ \mathrm{m}$ (negative, because the segment is below the time axis).

lessonAssessment.question: A velocity-time graph starts at $+10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and falls along a straight line to $0$ at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$, then continues along the same line to $-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$. Which statement is correct?
choices: The acceleration changes sign at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ because the velocity does.
The acceleration is $-2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ for the whole $0$-to-$6\ \mathrm{s}$ interval.
The acceleration is zero at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ because the velocity is zero there.

feedback.correct: Correct — it is one straight line, so one constant slope: $\Delta v / \Delta t = (-5 - 10)/(6 - 0) = -15/6 = -2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ throughout.

incorrect.0: The line does not bend at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ — same slope before and after. The velocity changing sign does not make the slope change sign.
incorrect.2: The slope of the line at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ is the same as everywhere else on it. A zero *velocity* does not mean a zero *slope*.
incorrect.3: The area from $4$ to $6\ \mathrm{s}$ is below the axis and negative. Above: $\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(10) = +20\ \mathrm{m}$; below: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(5) = -5\ \mathrm{m}$; net $= +15\ \mathrm{m}$.

hint: It is a single straight line from $(0, +10)$ to $(6, -5)$. How many different slopes does one straight line have?
lessonAssessment.solution: The graph is one straight line, so it has one slope: $\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{(-5) - (+10)}{6 - 0} = \dfrac{-15}{6} = -2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, constant over the whole interval. The velocity passing through zero at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ does not change the slope.

lessonAssessment.scenario:
Take east as positive. A robot's velocity-time graph is made of three straight segments:

| Segment | Interval | Velocity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0$ s to $4$ s | constant $+6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |
| 2 | $4$ s to $8$ s | straight line from $+6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |
| 3 | $8$ s to $12$ s | constant $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |

parts.prompt: (a) Find the robot's acceleration on each segment. Show $\Delta v$, $\Delta t$, and the sign.
parts.modelResponse: Segment 1: horizontal, $\Delta v = 0$, so $a_1 = 0$. Segment 2: $\Delta v = (-2) - (+6) = -8\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $\Delta t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$, $a_2 = -8/4 = -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Segment 3: horizontal, $\Delta v = 0$, so $a_3 = 0$.

parts.prompt: (b) Find the displacement during each segment (use area; segment 2 is a rectangle plus a triangle, or split at the zero crossing).
parts.modelResponse: Segment 1: $(+6)(4) = +24\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 2: the line crosses zero at $t = 7\ \mathrm{s}$ (three-quarters of the way). Above the axis, $0$ to $3\ \mathrm{s}$ into the segment: triangle $\tfrac12(3)(6) = +9\ \mathrm{m}$. Below the axis, last $1\ \mathrm{s}$: triangle $\tfrac12(1)(2) = -1\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 2 total: $+9 + (-1) = +8\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 3: $(-2)(4) = -8\ \mathrm{m}$.

parts.prompt: (c) Find the robot's net displacement over the full $12\ \mathrm{s}$, and describe where it ends up relative to the start.
parts.modelResponse: Net $= (+24) + (+8) + (-8) = +24\ \mathrm{m}$. The robot finishes $24\ \mathrm{m}$ east of where it started.

parts.prompt: (d) A student says segment 2 shows the robot “accelerating, then decelerating” because the velocity is positive then negative. Explain what is wrong.
parts.modelResponse: Segment 2 is a single straight line, so the acceleration is one constant value, $-2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, the whole time — it never switches between “accelerating” and “decelerating.” What changes is the relationship between velocity and acceleration: while $v > 0$ the object slows (a opposes v); at $v = 0$ it is momentarily at rest; while $v < 0$ it speeds up (a and v now agree). The slope — the acceleration — is unchanged throughout.

examConnection: Reading acceleration from a velocity-time slope and displacement from its signed area — including regions below the axis — is standard AP and IB Paper 1 material, and the “match the description to the graph” task recurs across kinematics. This lesson also sets up free fall, where the velocity-time graph is a single straight line through zero.
summary: On a velocity-time graph, the slope of a segment is the acceleration ($\Delta v / \Delta t$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$) — unchanged through a zero-velocity crossing — and the signed area between the graph and the time axis is the displacement: a rectangle for constant velocity, a triangle for constant acceleration, negative below the axis, combined as a signed sum. To match a description to a graph, check sign, constancy, and pattern of change one at a time.

exitQuestion.question: Two velocity-time graphs cover the same $0$-to-$10\ \mathrm{s}$ interval. Graph P is horizontal at $+2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Graph Q is a straight line from $+6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ down to $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Which quantities must be equal for the two motions?

feedback.correct: Correct — Graph P's area is $(2)(10) = +20\ \mathrm{m}$. Graph Q's area is a triangle above ($\tfrac12 \cdot 7.5 \cdot 6 = +22.5$) plus a triangle below ($\tfrac12 \cdot 2.5 \cdot 2 = -2.5$), net $+20\ \mathrm{m}$. Equal displacements.

incorrect.0: Graph P has zero slope; Graph Q has slope $-0.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Different accelerations.
incorrect.2: At $t = 5\ \mathrm{s}$, Graph P reads $+2\ \mathrm{m/s}$; Graph Q reads $+2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ as well — but this is a coincidence of these numbers, not something that *must* be equal for the described motions in general. The guaranteed equality is the displacement (equal signed area).
incorrect.3: Graph P ends at $+2\ \mathrm{m/s}$; Graph Q ends at $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Different final velocities.

hint: Displacement is the area between the graph and the time axis. Compare the two areas.
exitQuestion.solution: Displacement is the signed area. Graph P: $(+2\ \mathrm{m/s})(10\ \mathrm{s}) = +20\ \mathrm{m}$. Graph Q (straight line from $+6$ to $-2$ over $10\ \mathrm{s}$, crossing zero at $t = 7.5\ \mathrm{s}$): area above $= \tfrac12(7.5)(6) = +22.5\ \mathrm{m}$; area below $= \tfrac12(2.5)(2) = -2.5\ \mathrm{m}$; net $= +20\ \mathrm{m}$. The displacements are equal; the accelerations and final velocities are not.
